events.title: Out of Taiwan
events.text: Scholars think the ancestors of the Polynesians began sailing out from Taiwan and island Southeast Asia roughly 5,000 years ago. The family tree of their languages points back to Taiwan. So does the DNA of wauke, the paper mulberry they carried for making cloth.

events.title: The Lapita voyagers
events.text: People who made a stamped pottery called Lapita appear in the Bismarck Archipelago, near New Guinea. Starting around 1200 BCE they push east into open ocean, reaching Vanuatu, Fiji, Tonga, and Samoa. Coral tools date the first landing in Tonga to about 2,800 years ago. Their canoes carried crop plants, pigs, dogs, and chickens.

events.title: The long pause
events.text: For many centuries the voyagers stayed around Tonga and Samoa. Here, scholars think, Polynesian language and culture took shape. Nobody knows for sure why they waited so long. Some researchers think new sailing technology finally opened the way east.

events.title: A burst into East Polynesia
events.text: Then everything sped up. A careful review of more than 1,400 radiocarbon dates puts the first settlers in the Society Islands, the home of Tahiti, around 1025 to 1120 CE. Within about two centuries canoes had reached nearly every island in East Polynesia, from Hawaiʻi to Rapa Nui to Aotearoa.

events.title: Landfall in Hawaiʻi
events.text: Voyagers reach Hawaiʻi with their plants and animals. Archaeologist Patrick Kirch places the arrival between about 1000 and 1200 CE. Another team narrows it to around 940 to 1130 CE, while a third study points to the 1200s. Older books say 300 to 750 CE, but those dates came from samples like old wood that can fool the test. Most archaeologists have dropped them.

events.title: A meeting with South America
events.text: DNA from living Polynesians shows that Polynesians and Native Americans met and had children together around 1200 CE. Many researchers think this contact is how ʻuala, the sweet potato, got into the canoe plant family. Experts still argue about the details.

events.title: Round trips to Kahiki
events.text: Oral traditions tell of chiefs and priests sailing back and forth between Hawaiʻi and Kahiki, the homeland to the south. Moʻikeha sailed from Tahiti and settled on Kauaʻi, and his son Kila sailed south again to fetch Laʻamaikahiki. The priest Paʻao came north and brought the chief Pili. After that, the traditions say, the long voyages stopped.

events.title: The isolation ends
events.text: Captain James Cook reaches Kauaʻi and Niʻihau. He sees chickens already living on Kauaʻi and leaves English pigs on Niʻihau. From this point on, new plants and animals pour into Hawaiʻi from all over the world. That is why 1778 is the line between canoe plants and everything that came later.

events.title: Hōkūleʻa sails to Tahiti
events.text: Some writers had claimed Polynesians only drifted to their islands by accident. On May 1, 1976, the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa left Maui to test that. Master navigator Mau Piailug of Satawal, in Micronesia, guided her with no instruments, using stars, sun, and swells. She reached Tahiti on June 4, and more than 17,000 people came to greet her.

events.title: A Hawaiian navigator again
events.text: Nainoa Thompson, a student of Mau Piailug, navigates Hōkūleʻa from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti and back without instruments. He is the first Hawaiian in centuries to do it. He measured the height of stars with nothing but his outstretched hand.

events.title: Mālama Honua, around the world
events.text: Hōkūleʻa sails more than 40,000 nautical miles around the planet on the Mālama Honua voyage. The name means to care for our Earth. She came home to Oʻahu on June 17, 2017.

events.title: Moananuiākea, around the Pacific
events.text: Hōkūleʻa and her sister canoe Hikianalia launch the Moananuiākea voyage from Juneau, Alaska, on June 15, 2023. The plan is about 43,000 nautical miles around the whole Pacific. The canoes came home for a while after the 2023 Maui fires and rough El Niño weather, then set out again. By late 2025 they had reached Aotearoa.

howWeKnow.title: Radiocarbon dating
howWeKnow.text: Living things take in carbon, and a tiny part of it slowly ticks away after they die, like a clock. By measuring what is left in a burnt seed or twig, scientists can tell how old a campsite is. The trick is to test things that lived a short time. An old log can make a site look centuries too old, which is how the early dates for Hawaiʻi went wrong.

howWeKnow.title: Plant DNA
howWeKnow.text: Wauke was grown from cuttings, so each plant is a copy of its parent, and its DNA works like a shipping label. Wauke across the Pacific carries a label that traces back to Taiwan. Old ʻuala samples saved in museum plant collections match sweet potatoes from the Peru and Ecuador region. One team argues that sweet potato seeds could have crossed the ocean without people, so this debate is still alive.

howWeKnow.title: Language
howWeKnow.text: Words travel with the things they name. Across Polynesia the sweet potato is called kumara, kumala, or something close. Hawaiian ʻuala comes from that same old word. In Quechua, a language of the Andes in South America, the word for sweet potato sounds almost the same, cumal or kumara. Many researchers see that as a clue that the plant and its name were handed over together.

howWeKnow.title: Oral tradition
howWeKnow.text: Chants, genealogies, and moʻolelo remember named navigators, named canoes, and sailing routes between Hawaiʻi and Kahiki. For a long time outsiders brushed these stories off. Then Hōkūleʻa sailed the route in 1976 using only traditional wayfinding and showed that the voyages in the stories could really be done.
